old: L' is the elided article (il/la → l') before a vowel: l'uomo, l'amica. Gender is hidden by elision.
focus: Elision hides gender – anchor on l'acqua itself (is it il or la?); keep at most one sibling example

old: 'Abitare' = to live (somewhere). 'In centro' = downtown/in the center. 'In' without article before general areas.
focus: One rule only: 'in centro' takes no article – English says 'in the center'; cut the abitare gloss

old: 'Amare' = to love (stronger than 'piacere'). 'La musica' uses the article – Italian uses definite articles with abstract nouns.
focus: Definite article with things loved in general – 'amo la musica' where English drops 'the'; cut the amare-vs-piacere aside

old: 'Giocare a' + sport: 'gioco a tennis'. Use 'a' before sports. 'Giocare' has a soft g before -o: 'gioco'.
focus: 'Giocare a' + sport ('gioco a tennis') – English 'play tennis' has no preposition; cut the soft-g spelling aside

old: Reflexive verbs need a pronoun: `mi chiamo` (I call myself = my name is), `si lava` (he washes himself). The pronoun matches the subject – mi/ti/si/ci/vi/si.
focus: Anchor on 'ti alzi' – alzarsi is literally 'raise yourself' = get up; pronoun matches subject; strip backticks and off-card examples

old: Endings hint at gender: -o usually m, -a usually f. But la mano is f, il problema is m. The article is the real signal.
focus: Good insight (the article, not the ending, is the real gender signal) – anchor it on 'la pasta è pronta' with its double -a agreement

old: Sapere (to know facts) is irregular: so, sai, sa, sappiamo, sapete, sanno. Compare with conoscere (to know people/places).
focus: Keep only sapere = know facts vs conoscere = know people/places, anchored on 'sai la risposta'; drop the paradigm list

old: `stare` for how you are right now: `come stai?` (how are you?), `sto bene` (I'm fine). With permanent traits switch to `essere`.
focus: Stare for current states/attention – anchor on 'non stai attento'; strip backticks

old: Yes/no questions in Italian mainly use rising intonation. Word order can stay the same, though subject-verb inversion is also possible for emphasis.
focus: Anchor on 'Puoi ripetere?' – statement word order + rising intonation makes the yes/no question; cut the hedgy inversion aside

old: "Stare + gerundio" forms the Italian progressive: "sto parlando" (I am speaking right now).
focus: Progressive = stare + -ndo; anchor on this card's 'sta cucinando' instead of sto parlando

old: Reflexive isn't always literal in English: `ricordarsi` = to remember, `arrabbiarsi` = to get angry. If the dictionary form ends in -si, you need the matching pronoun.
focus: Second reflexive telling, new angle: 'mi lavo i denti' – reflexive + article replaces the possessive (i denti, not 'my' teeth); strip backticks and off-card examples

old: After expressions of wish/doubt/opinion + `che`, Italian uses subjunctive (congiuntivo). `Voglio che tu venga` (not vieni) = 'I want you to come'.
focus: Doubt/opinion + che triggers subjunctive – anchor on 'Credo che... sia partita'; strip backticks and the off-card venga example

old: Modal verbs (dovere, potere, volere) attach directly to the infinitive: `devo studiare`, `posso aiutare`, `voglio mangiare`. No preposition needed – unlike English's clunkier 'have to' / 'be able to'.
focus: Modal + bare infinitive is the right insight – anchor on 'posso cambiare'; strip backticks; trim example pile

old: 'Camminare al parco' = to walk to the park. 'Al' = a+il (contraction). All -are 'noi' forms: -iamo.
focus: One rule only: al = a + il contraction, anchored on 'al parco'; cut the gloss and the -iamo conjugation aside

english: They say it would rain tomorrow.
old: Conditional used for reported/unconfirmed info.
focus: Reportative conditional is a real surprise – anchor on 'pioverebbe': 'they say it would rain' = unconfirmed report; add a hook, it's currently a bare label

english: It would be better to leave early.
old: Conditional of essere + meglio for giving advice.
focus: 'Sarebbe meglio' + infinitive is the polite-advice softener ('it would be better to') – quote the card's phrase and add a hook; current tip is a bare label.

old: 'Lungo' as preposition means 'along': 'cammino lungo il fiume' = I walk along the river.
focus: lungo = 'long' as adjective but 'along' as preposition – lead with the two-meanings landmine, cut the sentence re-translation.

old: 'Vicino a' = near/close to: 'abitiamo vicino al parco'. Note 'a+il' contracts to 'al'. Opposite: 'lontano da'.
focus: English 'near the park' takes no preposition but Italian needs vicino A ('vicino al parco') – one rule; drop the lontano da add-on.

english: She gets ready to go out.
old: Reflexive verbs use 'si' for third person: 'si prepara' = she gets (herself) ready. Full pattern: mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si.
focus: 'si prepara' = she prepares HERSELF – Italian makes daily-routine verbs reflexive where English doesn't; cut the mi/ti/si/ci/vi/si paradigm list.

english: In the evening I watch a movie.
old: Definite article with days/times for habits: 'il lunedì lavoro' = on Mondays I work. No article = one specific day.
focus: The article on time phrases means habitual: 'La sera guardo un film' = in the evenings, every evening – anchor in THIS card's 'La sera', not the sibling 'il lunedì' example.

target: La metro passa ogni cinque minuti.
english: The metro comes every five minutes.
old: 'Ogni' (every/each) is always singular: 'ogni cinque minuti' = every five minutes. Never changes form.
focus: ogni never changes form, and with a numeral it takes a plural noun: 'ogni cinque minuti' – fix the misleading 'always singular' claim that contradicts the card's own plural 'minuti'.

target: Noi passiamo le vacanze al mare.
english: We spend the holidays at the beach.
old: 'Passare le vacanze' = to spend holidays. 'Al mare' = at the seaside. 'Al' = a+il (contraction).
focus: 'Spending' time is passare, never spendere (money only): 'passiamo le vacanze' – lead with that trap, cut the al-contraction and seaside glosses.

old: "Stare" describes temporary states and conditions: "sta bene" (is well), "sta attento" (is paying attention).
focus: stare for how you're doing/feeling – anchor with this card's 'sta peggio' (she's doing worse) instead of the sibling sta bene/sta attento examples.

old: If a reflexive verb follows a modal, the pronoun can sit before the modal OR attach to the infinitive: `mi devo alzare` = `devo alzarmi`. Both valid; sound the same.
focus: The pronoun can sit before the modal or attach to the infinitive: 'Mi puoi aiutare' = 'Puoi aiutarmi', both fine – fix the wrong 'reflexive' label (aiutare isn't reflexive here), use this card, no backticks.

old: WH-question with 'cosa/che cosa' (what): Cos'hai = cosa + hai (elision). Past tense question.
focus: Decode the contraction: Cos'hai = cosa + hai, elision before a vowel – drop the 'WH-question' and 'past tense question' labels.

old: `stare + gerundio` = English '-ing now': `sto mangiando` = 'I'm eating (right now)'. Italian uses it less than English – bare present often does the job.
focus: 'sto cercando' = I'm looking right now (stare + gerund), but Italian uses it far less than English -ing – keep that usage note, anchor in this card's phrase, remove backticks.

old: Only use `stare + -ando/-endo` for emphasis on 'this very moment'. `Mangio adesso` and `sto mangiando adesso` both work; the gerundio adds 'in progress'.
focus: Progressive is optional emphasis in Italian – 'stai leggendo' stresses in-progress, bare present would also work – anchor in this card's phrase, remove backticks and the sibling mangiando example.

target: Io sto attento a quello che mangio.
english: I'm careful about what I eat.
old: Health, mood, brief states → `stare`. `Sto male` = I'm not feeling well (today). `Sono malato` = I'm ill (a condition).
focus: stare for states you're in vs essere for what you are – keep the sto male/sono malato contrast but anchor in this card's 'sto attento' first, remove backticks.

old: Past tense with movement/change verbs uses `essere`: `sono andato` (I went), `è arrivata` (she arrived). The participle agrees with the subject: -o/-a/-i/-e.
focus: 'sono nato' is literally 'I am born' – nascere takes essere in the past and the participle agrees – quote this card's nato, remove backticks and sibling examples.

old: Auxiliary `essere` triggers agreement: a woman says `sono andata`, men say `sono andato`. With `avere` no agreement (almost ever).
focus: 'sei nata' ends in -a because 'you' is a woman – essere participles agree with the subject – use this card's nata as the example, remove backticks.

english: What time do you wake up?
old: Reflexive isn't always literal in English: `ricordarsi` = to remember, `arrabbiarsi` = to get angry. If the dictionary form ends in -si, you need the matching pronoun.
focus: svegliarsi ends in -si, so it needs the matching pronoun: 'ti svegli' – reflexives aren't literal 'self' actions in English – anchor in this card, remove backticks and sibling verbs.

old: `piacere` works backwards from English: the thing that pleases is the subject. `Mi piace la pizza` literally = 'pizza is pleasing to me'. Plural thing? Use `piacciono`: `mi piacciono i libri`.
focus: piacere works backwards – 'Ti piace l'Italia' = Italy pleases you – re-anchor in THIS card (not mi piace la pizza), remove backticks; this is telling 1 of the piacere budget (intro angle).

old: WH-question with 'perché' (why): Perché sei triste? = Why are you sad? 'Perché' also means 'because' in answers.
focus: perché is both 'why' and 'because' – the same word asks the question and starts the answer – cut the re-translation padding.

old: Don't say `io piaccio la pizza` – that means 'I'm pleasing to pizza'. The Italian flips: pizza does the pleasing. Match the verb to the thing, not to you.
focus: Content is strong – the 'io piaccio la pizza' warning already anchors to this card's pizza – only remove backticks and tighten; telling 2 of the piacere budget (error-warning angle).

old: "Lo" is used before masculine nouns starting with s+consonant, z, gn, ps, x: lo studente, lo zaino.
focus: The s+consonant rule is correct for this card – make 'lo specchio' the worked example instead of the sibling lo studente/lo zaino.

old: Same trap as Spanish `gustar`. `Piace` for singular, `piacciono` for plural. The 'liker' becomes the indirect object (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi).
focus: piacciono for plural things – anchor in 'ti piacciono i miei quadri' (the paintings do the pleasing); drop the Spanish gustar reference and backticks

target: Ci sono due camere da letto.
old: C'è = there is (singular), ci sono = there are (plural). "Ci" is a locative pronoun meaning "there".
focus: c'e vs ci sono, anchored in 'ci sono due camere' – say ci literally means 'there' in plain words, no 'locative pronoun' jargon

target: Ci sono tanti ristoranti in centro.
old: Quantity adjectives (molto, poco, troppo, tanto, quanto) agree in gender and number with the noun.
focus: quantity words inflect – use the card's 'tanti ristoranti' as the worked example instead of the bare molto/poco list

target: Mi piace fare colazione al bar.
english: I like having breakfast at the cafe.
old: `piacere` works backwards from English: the thing that pleases is the subject. `Mi piace la pizza` literally = 'pizza is pleasing to me'. Plural thing? Use `piacciono`: `mi piacciono i libri`.
focus: piace + infinitive stays singular: 'mi piace fare colazione' – the activity is the subject; strip backticks and the generic pizza stamp

old: These all take `avere`: fame, sete, sonno, freddo, caldo, paura, fretta, ragione, torto, voglia, anni. Saying `sono fame` is wrong – you'd be hunger itself.
focus: she HAS cold, not is cold – anchor 'ha freddo', keep the sono-freddo warning, trim the eleven-noun list, no backticks

target: Ci sono molte persone al mercato.
english: There are many people at the market.
old: Don't say `c'è due mele` – once you go plural, you need `ci sono`. Past tense: `c'era / c'erano`. Future: `ci sarà / ci saranno`.
focus: once plural you need ci sono – anchor 'ci sono molte persone'; cut the past/future tense inventory and backticks, one rule only

old: Physical description adjectives agree in gender/number with the noun they describe and usually follow it.
focus: adjective agrees with its noun: la ragazza e alta (fem -a) – drop the 'usually follows the noun' clause, which this predicative sentence does not show

old: Passato prossimo with essere: the past participle agrees in gender/number with the subject. Sono andata (f).
focus: essere-verbs make the participle agree – anchor 'siamo caduti' (-i for we) instead of the off-card sono andata example

old: Passato prossimo: auxiliary 'avere' + past participle (-ato, -uto, -ito). Most transitive verbs use 'avere'.
focus: avere + participle = simple past, anchored in 'hai chiamato' – say helper verb, not 'auxiliary'

target: Nevicava molto e abbiamo chiuso le scuole.
english: It was snowing a lot and we closed the schools.
old: Imperfetto vs passato prossimo: imperfetto for ongoing/background actions, passato prossimo for completed/sudden events. "Dormivo (background) quando è suonato (sudden event)."
focus: background vs event is IN this card – anchor 'nevicava' (background) + 'abbiamo chiuso' (event), replace the off-card dormivo example

target: La settimana scorsa ho lavorato tanto.
english: Last week I worked a lot.
old: Most verbs use 'avere' as auxiliary: 'Ho mangiato' (I ate). Movement verbs use 'essere': 'Sono andato'.
focus: avere vs essere choice anchored in 'ho lavorato' (avere), keep sono andato as the movement contrast – say helper verb, not 'auxiliary'
